chunks: Muhammad narrated from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadhr, from Amr ibn Shimir, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

When Allah the Exalted revealed to His Messenger (peace be upon him and his family): 'Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, stone idols, and divination arrows are defilement from the work of Satan,' it was asked: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is al-maysir?' He said: 'Everything that is played with using dice, even the knucklebones and walnuts.' It was asked: 'What are al-an'sab?' He said: 'What they sacrificed for their idols.' It was asked: 'And what are al-azlam?' He said: 'Their arrows that they used for divination.' Then: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Abu al-Qasim al-Sayqal said: I wrote to him [the Imam] asking about the lists of swords that are called as-safan, which I make from fish skins; is it permissible to use them? And we do not eat their meat. He said: 'There is no harm.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Abu al-Qasim al-Sayqal said: I wrote to him asking about the lists of swords that are called as-safan, which I make from fish skins; is it permissible to use them? And we do not eat their meat. He said: 'There is no harm.'

key_terms.الْأَنْصَابُ: Idols or stone statues to which sacrifices were made
key_terms.الْمَيْسِرُ: Gambling or games of chance, specifically those involving dice or knucklebones

ai.seo_question: What is the definition of Maysir and Azlam in Shia jurisprudence according to the Imams?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq clarifies the specific pre-Islamic practices condemned in Surah Al-Ma'idah, defining 'al-maysir' broadly to include games of chance like dice and knucklebones, 'al-an'sab' as idols, and 'al-azlam' as divination arrows. It is followed by a distinct legal ruling on the permissibility of using fish skins for sword scabbards, illustrating the Shia juristic approach to applying purity rules to items where the source animal is not consumed.
